eligibility_reason: The agent's own interaction logs are rendered into images and stored verbatim in an external memory bank M = {(I_i, {s_i,k}, pi_i)} at run time (p. 4, Eq. 5); a query-time module g_theta reads M and returns supporting segments injected into the primary agent's context on later steps (p. 4, Eq. 6), and the paper frames this as reusing 'experience accumulated over extended histories' across a 'continuous stream of tasks' (p. 1). This is an LLM-based agent writing and later retrieving cross-turn state, satisfying I1. Year is 2026 (arXiv:2604.26622, p. 1), English, and full text was retrievable. No exclusion criterion applies: the store is written by the agent itself (not E3), it is an externalised store beyond parametric weights (not E2), it is a primary empirical study, not a survey (not E4), memory is the entire contribution rather than incidental (not E5), and the paper spans at least 13 pages (not E7).

facets.justification: The store is a bank of rendered, SoM-annotated trajectory images paired with verbatim text segments and metadata (p. 4, Eq. 5: M = {m_i}, m_i = (I_i, {s_i,k}, pi_i)), retrieved by a fine-tuned vision-language relevance model rather than by embedding similarity, graph traversal, SQL, or plain file access. The paper's own framing is that this optical/visual representation is the novel contribution distinguishing it from vector, graph, relational, or filesystem stores (p. 1 abstract; p. 2, 'renders historical trajectories into images annotated with unique visual identifiers'), so none of the named categories fit without distortion.

Beyond storing new trajectory chunks, the paper's central write-side mechanism is an age-aware adaptive-resolution scheme: 'an older memory is assigned to a higher aging tier, which in turn dictates a lower image resolution' (p. 5, Eq. 13), explicitly termed 'optical forgetting' that 'significantly reduces the visual-token cost of long-term history' (p. 5). This is a condensation of stored representation over time/overflow, the defining feature of summarize_compress, not a simple unmodified append.

Retrieval combines a probability-threshold filter with a Top-K fallback under a stated union rule: S_i(q) = {(i,k) : p_i,k(q) >= tau} union TopK({p_i,k(q)}, K) (p. 4, Eq. 12), which the text itself calls a 'hybrid selection strategy' that 'robustly maintains coverage... without manual tuning' (p. 5). The fusion rule is declared, not incidental, satisfying the guide's bar for hybrid.

The system is assessed via 'empirical evaluations on the Mind2Web... and AppWorld... benchmarks' against baselines and ablations (p. 2), with backbone-generalization and retrieval-quality tables reported on public benchmarks (p. 9, Tables 5-7). No real users, fielded deployment, or setting with stakes outside the authors' own experiments is described anywhere in the given pages, so this is a novel technique investigated in the lab rather than evaluation in practice.

Results are reported as scores over fixed task suites and baselines: Table 5 (Mind2Web backbone generalization vs. Text-RAG), Table 6 (Recall@1/5/10, MRR on an Experience Retrieval Evaluation Subset), and Table 7 (system efficiency profile on Mind2Web) (p. 9).

The paper repeatedly self-identifies the contribution as an architecture rather than a single technique: 'we propose Optical Context Retrieval Memory (OCR-Memory), a memory framework' (p. 1 abstract), and the contributions list opens with 'We propose OCR-Memory, the first memory framework to store an agent's interaction history in the image modality' (p. 2), organizing multiple sub-mechanisms (locate-and-transcribe retrieval, multi-resolution storage, training strategy) under one system.
